title: Zero Pivots, Rank and Singularity
quickIdea: The number of nonzero entries on the diagonal of U is the rank of A, so a lost dimension and a zero pivot are the same fact seen twice.
remember: rank(A) equals the number of nonzero pivots in U, and the same holds for the pivots of PA = LU.
A is singular exactly when some u_ii = 0, exactly when det(U) = 0, exactly when det(A) = 0.
A is invertible exactly when every u_ii is nonzero; then L and U are both invertible, because L is unit triangular with det 1 and det(U) = det(A).
A zero pivot *during* elimination is not the same as a zero pivot at the end: the first may only mean a row swap is needed, the second means the matrix is singular.
Singularity is a statement about A. Whether Ax = b has no solution or infinitely many is a statement about [A|b], and needs the augmented matrix.

example.prompt: Factor A = [[1,2],[2,4]] and read off its rank and singularity.
example.work: R2 <- R2 - 2 R1 gives U = [[1,2],[0,0]] with L = [[1,0],[2,1]]. One pivot is 1, the other is 0.
example.answer: rank(A) = 1 and A is singular, since det(A) = 1*0 = 0. The zero pivot is in the last position, so no row swap was needed and no swap could have helped.

gateAngle: GATE CSE 2025 Set 2 Q.34 is built entirely on this card. Statement 2 (invertible P forces invertible L and U) and statement 3 (singular P forces a zero on U's diagonal) are both the identity det(P) = det(L) det(U) read in one direction or the other. The answer is that statements 1, 2 and 3 are true and 4 is false.

variations.label: ORIGINAL PYQ-STYLE QUESTION
variations.question: U = [[2,1,0],[0,0,3],[0,0,1]] comes from a factorization with no row exchange. What is rank(A), and is A invertible?
variations.answer: rank(A) = 2 and A is not invertible, because the diagonal of U is 2, 0, 1.
variations.why: Two nonzero pivots out of three, so one dimension is lost; the zero pivot is enough to make det(U) = 0 whatever the off-diagonal entries are.

variations.label: CONCEPTUAL PRACTICE QUESTION
variations.question: Why is a unit lower triangular matrix always invertible, whatever its entries below the diagonal?
variations.answer: Because its determinant is the product of its diagonal, which is 1*1*...*1 = 1, and a matrix with nonzero determinant is invertible.
variations.why: This is what lets statement 2 of the 2025 question be settled by looking at U alone: L never causes a singularity.

variations.label: PREDICTED VARIATION
variations.question: A is 5x5 with rank 5 and has a factorization PA = LU. Can any u_ii be zero?
variations.answer: No. rank(A) = 5 means five nonzero pivots, so all five diagonal entries of U are nonzero and U is invertible.
variations.why: Rank and the pivot count are the same number, and with full rank every pivot is available.

trap.what: Reading a zero on the diagonal of U as 'the system has no solution'.
trap.why: A zero pivot says A is singular, which leaves two possibilities: no solution or infinitely many, depending on the right-hand side. Which one it is depends on rank([A|b]), not on U alone.
trap.counterexample: A = [[1,2],[2,4]] with b = (1,2) has infinitely many solutions, because the second equation is twice the first. The same A with b = (1,3) has none, because 2x + 4y = 3 contradicts 2x + 4y = 2. Both have u22 = 0.

check.question: For a symmetric P = LU with L unit lower triangular, is L symmetric? Is U?
check.answer: Not in general. A lower triangular matrix that equals its transpose must be diagonal, and a unit diagonal makes it the identity, which would force P to be diagonal.
check.explanation: That is why statement 4 of GATE CSE 2025 Set 2 Q.34 is false, and why the right factorization for a symmetric matrix is LDL^T rather than symmetric L and U.
